title: The serpent who holds the world
hookLine: Shesha holds up the whole earth without strain, and Patanjali's seat is steady and easy
carry: asana: a seat both steady and easy
last: SANTOSHA: NOTHING IS HIGHER THAN ENOUGH.

lines: A SERPENT WITH A THOUSAND HOODS.
cards: Between one age of the world and the next, the Puranas say, there is only ocean, and on it floats a vast serpent with a thousand hoods, coiled like a bed. Vishnu rests on him.
His name is Shesha, also called Ananta, the endless, and in the Vishnu Purana he carries the whole earth on his hoods: mountains, seas, cities, everyone. He doesn't strain. He doesn't drop it.
Only when he yawns, the text says, does the earth tremble. Remember him from the start of the week? The tradition says Patanjali was Shesha come down.
So what did the serpent teach about sitting?

teach.b: Three short sutras. Sutra 2.46: sthira sukham asanam. Sthira, steady.
Sukha, easy, comfortable. Asana, seat, from a root meaning to sit. Not rigid.

teach.h: RELAX THE EFFORT, REST IN THE ENDLESS.
teach.b: Sutra 2.47 says how: by relaxing effort, and letting the mind rest in the endless, ananta. Some commentators hear the serpent in that word: Shesha, holding the world steady and easy, is a picture of the seat.

teach.h: NO LONGER KNOCKED BY THE PAIRS.
teach.b: Sutra 2.48 gives the result: then you're not knocked about by the pairs, heat and cold, comfort and discomfort. That's all it says.

The classical commentary adds a few names of seats, the lotus and the hero's seat among them, but no sequence and no instructions. The long lists of postures belong to later hatha yoga texts and to modern teachers.
That doesn't make them wrong. It shows what Patanjali was after: a body quiet enough to forget, so the inner limbs can begin. Hindus still use the word this way.
In puja, the asana is the seat or small mat you sit on before the shrine, and a steady, easy seat is where japa and prayer happen.
Now look back over the week. Indra kept going back. The serpent came down to teach eight limbs.
Parvati's fire. Deer that don't run. Dhruva's husks.
And today, a seat. A week of the outer limbs, and almost none of it was about the body.

how: In the Yoga Sutras, asana is the seated posture for meditation, steady and easy; in puja the asana is the seat or mat the worshipper sits on, Hindus who meditate or do japa often sit cross-legged on one, and modern posture classes draw on later hatha yoga traditions.

o: good: steadiness is all that matters.
it needs to be easy too, steady and comfortable at once.

games.why: sthira sukham asanam: steady and comfortable, both. 2.47 adds: by relaxing effort.

practice: Find a seat, chair, cushion or floor, and make it steady: the spine rising a little, the base settling down.

Then make it easy: drop the shoulders, unclench the jaw, soften the hands, and let whatever's under you do the holding, the way Shesha holds the world. When an itch or ache asks for attention, notice it like weather.

wordCard.voice: Asana. The seat, the third limb of yoga, which Patanjali describes in three words: steady and comfortable.

orig.note: Sanskrit āsana: seat, from the root ās, to sit; in 2.46, sthira-sukham āsanam.

carryVoice: Your line: asana, a seat both steady and easy, like Shesha holding the earth without strain. A week of outer limbs, done.
